ripple_effect.name: Sanctions imposed on a major economy

historical_precedents.event: Western sanctions on Russia following its invasion of Ukraine
historical_precedents.what_happened: The U.S., EU, and allies imposed sweeping sanctions on Russia's financial system, energy exports, and access to Western technology, and froze a large share of Russia's foreign-currency reserves.
historical_precedents.market_impact: European natural gas prices spiked to record highs as Russian pipeline gas supply to Europe fell sharply over the following year, and European governments spent heavily to secure alternative energy supplies and shield consumers from higher bills.

historical_precedents.event: International sanctions on Iran over its nuclear program
historical_precedents.what_happened: A series of U.S. and international sanctions restricted Iran's ability to sell oil and access the global banking system.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Iranian oil exports fell sharply, though global oil prices were also affected by supply from other producers filling the gap; Iran's own currency and economy experienced significant strain during the most restrictive sanctions periods.

possibility_chains: Sanctions targeting a major energy or commodity exporter have historically tightened global supply of that commodity, which has often (though not always, depending on how much other producers can offset the loss) pushed prices higher.

Sanctioned countries have historically sought alternative trading partners and payment systems over time, a process that has typically reduced — but not eliminated — the sanctions' economic impact the longer they remain in place.
Countries or companies that depended heavily on trade with the sanctioned economy have historically faced their own adjustment costs, not just the sanctioned party.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: International sanctions on Iran over its nuclear program (2010s): Iranian oil exports fell sharply, though global oil prices were also affected by supply from other producers filling the gap; Iran's own currency and economy experienced significant strain during the most restrictive sanctions periods. Sanctions targeting a major energy or commodity exporter have historically tightened global supply of that commodity, which has often (though not always, depending on how much other producers can offset the loss) pushed prices higher.

ripple_effect.name: Persian Gulf oil supply shock

historical_precedents.event: Iran–Iraq "Tanker War"
historical_precedents.what_happened: Iran and Iraq attacked oil tankers transiting the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz, and Iran repeatedly threatened to close the strait.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Shipping insurance war-risk premiums in the Gulf rose sharply, and the U.S. Navy began escorting reflagged Kuwaiti tankers in 1987 to keep the strait open.

historical_precedents.event: Drone and missile attack on Saudi Aramco's Abqaiq and Khurais facilities
historical_precedents.what_happened: The attack (which Saudi Arabia and the U.S. blamed on Iran, a claim Iran denied) temporarily knocked out roughly half of Saudi Arabia's oil output, about 5% of global supply.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Brent crude jumped about 15% in a single day — the largest one-day oil price increase since the 1990–91 Gulf War.

historical_precedents.event: Gulf War (Iraqi invasion of Kuwait)
historical_precedents.what_happened: Iraq's invasion of Kuwait removed a large share of Gulf oil exports from the market and raised fears of a wider regional war.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Oil prices roughly doubled in the months following the invasion before falling back once the war ended and supply concerns eased.

possibility_chains: Roughly a fifth of the world's oil is estimated to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, so a sustained blockage or major disruption there has historically driven crude oil prices sharply higher.

Because ammonia-based fertilizer production is natural-gas intensive, and natural gas prices often move together with oil, a prolonged energy price spike has historically fed through into higher fertilizer costs over the following months.
Fertilizer is a major input cost in food production, so energy shocks of this kind have historically been followed — often with a lag — by higher food prices.
Shipping insurers have historically raised war-risk premiums for vessels transiting the Gulf during periods of heightened tension, adding to the landed cost of oil and other cargo.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Gulf War (Iraqi invasion of Kuwait) (1990–1991): Oil prices roughly doubled in the months following the invasion before falling back once the war ended and supply concerns eased. Roughly a fifth of the world's oil is estimated to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, so a sustained blockage or major disruption there has historically driven crude oil prices sharply higher.

ripple_effect.name: Government austerity program (spending cuts and tax rises)

historical_precedents.event: UK austerity programme under Chancellor George Osborne
historical_precedents.what_happened: Following his June 2010 budget, the Conservative-led coalition pursued roughly £110 billion in combined spending cuts and tax increases aimed at eliminating the structural deficit, including over £30 billion in welfare cuts, a 2011–2013 public sector pay freeze, and reductions that cut local government funding by an estimated 60% over the decade.
historical_precedents.market_impact: About 220,000 local authority jobs were eliminated and nearly 800 public libraries closed between 2010 and 2020; a 2017 University College London study published in BMJ Open found that annual health-funding growth fell from 3.8% in the 2000s to 0.41% after 2010, and researchers linked the slowdown in health and social care spending to a rise in mortality-rate growth over the same period.

historical_precedents.event: Canada's 1995 federal budget under Finance Minister Paul Martin
historical_precedents.what_happened: Facing a $30 billion federal deficit, Canada's budget cut program spending by a planned 18.9% by 1997–98, eliminated dozens of federal agencies and business subsidies (including a $560 million annual rail subsidy), and merged two separate federal transfer programs into a single, reduced Canada Health and Social Transfer block grant to the provinces.
historical_precedents.market_impact: By shrinking the federal transfer, the reform shifted fiscal pressure onto provincial governments, which had to make their own cuts to health and social assistance spending to absorb the reduced federal contribution.

possibility_chains: Government austerity programs that cut public sector employment have historically taken years to fully play out in local labor markets, as affected workers and the local businesses that served them adjust gradually rather than all at once.

Cuts concentrated in health and social services have historically been linked by researchers to slower improvement (or reversal) in public health outcomes, though isolating austerity's specific contribution from other factors has remained a subject of academic debate.

Federal-level austerity that reduces transfers to regional or local governments has historically pushed the political and fiscal burden of further cuts down to those lower levels of government, which have fewer tools (such as currency issuance or unlimited borrowing) to absorb the shortfall.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Canada's 1995 federal budget under Finance Minister Paul Martin (1995): By shrinking the federal transfer, the reform shifted fiscal pressure onto provincial governments, which had to make their own cuts to health and social assistance spending to absorb the reduced federal contribution. Government austerity programs that cut public sector employment have historically taken years to fully play out in local labor markets, as affected workers and the local businesses that served them adjust gradually rather than all at once.

linked_playbooks.name: IMF bailout or rescue program for a sovereign
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Sri Lanka's IMF Extended Fund Facility after its 2022 default (2022–2024): The program aimed to raise Sri Lanka's tax-to-GDP ratio from 8.1% in 2021 to 15% by 2025, but the accompanying austerity coincided with unemployment rising from 5.7% to 8.3% between 2022 and 2023. IMF rescue programs have historically come attached to austerity conditions (tax increases, spending cuts, structural reforms) that have often produced short-term economic pain — higher unemployment, reduced public services — even where they are intended to restore longer-term stability.

linked_playbooks.name: Eurozone periphery sovereign bond crisis
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Mario Draghi's 'whatever it takes' pledge (July 2012): The pledge is widely credited as the turning point in the crisis, prompting a steady decline in borrowing costs for Spain, Italy, and other periphery economies in the following months, even though the OMT program itself was never actually activated. Rising bond yields in one eurozone member has historically raised borrowing costs in other members seen as having similar debt vulnerabilities, a contagion dynamic distinct from a single-country crisis.

linked_playbooks.name: Pension/retirement-age reform triggers unrest
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: France's 2010 pension reform under President Sarkozy (September–October 2010): The strikes shut down all twelve of mainland France's oil refineries, leaving roughly one in four fuel stations dry nationwide, and cancelled about half of long-distance trains and up to 50% of flights at major airports before the government passed the reform largely unchanged. Government proposals to raise the statutory retirement age have historically triggered some of the largest and most sustained street protests and strikes a country experiences, often mobilizing unions well beyond those directly representing older workers.

linked_playbooks.name: Major municipal or county bankruptcy
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Jefferson County, Alabama bankruptcy (November 2011 – December 2013): The county cut its government workforce by more than 700 employees by May 2012, and the bankruptcy court wrote off more than $1.4 billion of the debt before the county emerged from bankruptcy in December 2013. A municipal bankruptcy driven by a shrinking tax base and rising legacy retiree costs has historically forced a choice between deep pension cuts and finding outside funding (such as philanthropic support) to soften them, since the two options are not fiscally separable.

ripple_effect.name: Diplomatic rupture between major regional powers

historical_precedents.event: Qatar diplomatic and blockade crisis
historical_precedents.what_happened: Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain, and Egypt severed diplomatic relations with Qatar on 5 June 2017 (Jordan followed a day later) and imposed a land, air, and sea blockade, accusing Qatar of supporting terrorism and being too close to Iran, allegations Qatar denied. The UAE banned Qatar-flagged vessels from its ports, which had previously handled over 85% of Qatar's cargo, and Qatar had to reroute Qatar Airways flights through Iranian airspace.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Qatar's stock market fell about 7.3% on the first day of the crisis and roughly 9.7% within days; S&P downgraded Qatar's sovereign credit rating from AA to AA-. The Qatari government injected an estimated $38.5 billion, about 23% of GDP, to stabilize the economy, and Qatar's GDP growth slowed to roughly -1.5% for 2017 before recovering to about 1.2% growth in 2018. The dispute was resolved at a January 2021 GCC summit in al-Ula, brokered by Kuwait and the U.S., restoring diplomatic and travel ties.

historical_precedents.event: Saudi Arabia severs relations with Iran
historical_precedents.what_happened: Saudi Arabia executed prominent Shia cleric Sheikh Nimr al-Nimr on 2 January 2016; when protesters in Tehran stormed and set fire to the Saudi embassy the next day, Saudi Arabia severed diplomatic relations with Iran on 3 January 2016 and gave Iranian diplomats 48 hours to leave.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The rupture deepened the broader Saudi-Iran regional rivalry playing out through proxy conflicts in Yemen, Syria, and elsewhere; relations were not restored until a China-brokered agreement announced 10 March 2023, with embassies reopening in Riyadh in June 2023 and Tehran in August 2023.

possibility_chains: A sudden severing of diplomatic relations between neighboring major economies has historically disrupted direct trade, aviation, and financial flows between them, forcing rerouting of commerce through third countries at added cost.

Blockades or embargoes imposed as part of a diplomatic rupture have historically prompted the isolated country to fast-track new trade relationships and, where relevant, domestic production to reduce dependence on the countries that cut ties.

Diplomatic ruptures between regional rivals have historically taken years, and often required third-party mediation, to fully resolve, even after the original triggering incident faded from headlines.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Saudi Arabia severs relations with Iran (January 2016): The rupture deepened the broader Saudi-Iran regional rivalry playing out through proxy conflicts in Yemen, Syria, and elsewhere; relations were not restored until a China-brokered agreement announced 10 March 2023, with embassies reopening in Riyadh in June 2023 and Tehran in August 2023. A sudden severing of diplomatic relations between neighboring major economies has historically disrupted direct trade, aviation, and financial flows between them, forcing rerouting of commerce through third countries at added cost.

linked_playbooks.name: Sanctions imposed on a major economy
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: International sanctions on Iran over its nuclear program (2010s): Iranian oil exports fell sharply, though global oil prices were also affected by supply from other producers filling the gap; Iran's own currency and economy experienced significant strain during the most restrictive sanctions periods. Sanctions targeting a major energy or commodity exporter have historically tightened global supply of that commodity, which has often (though not always, depending on how much other producers can offset the loss) pushed prices higher.

linked_playbooks.name: Coup or abrupt regime change disrupting trade relationships
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Myanmar military coup (February 2021): Foreign direct investment into Myanmar fell 22% to $3.8 billion in fiscal year 2020, and major foreign investors withdrew: Japan's Kirin ended a $1.7 billion brewery joint venture, Thailand's Amata halted a $1 billion industrial zone project, and India's Adani Ports terminated a $127 million port investment. The Yangon Stock Exchange suspended trading, and property sales reportedly dropped by nearly 100%. A coup in a country that is a significant exporter of a specific commodity has historically raised questions about the continuity of that country's mining, energy, or agricultural exports, even when physical production is not immediately disrupted.

ripple_effect.name: South China Sea territorial and shipping dispute

historical_precedents.event: Philippines v. China Permanent Court of Arbitration case
historical_precedents.what_happened: The Philippines brought a case to the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague in January 2013 challenging China's expansive 'nine-dash line' claim over most of the South China Sea. The tribunal ruled on 12 July 2016 that China's historic-rights claim had no lawful basis under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, and that none of the disputed Spratly Islands features qualified as islands generating their own exclusive economic zone.
historical_precedents.market_impact: China rejected the ruling as null and void and continued its island-building and patrol activities in the disputed waters. The ruling did not resolve the underlying dispute, and multiple claimant states (Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei, Taiwan) continue to assert overlapping claims to parts of the same waters, through which a large share of global seaborne trade transits.

possibility_chains: Escalation of naval or coast guard confrontations in the South China Sea has historically raised shipping insurers' and carriers' attention to route risk in a corridor that carries a very large share of world seaborne trade, given the absence, so far, of a sustained blockade in the disputed waters.

Legal rulings against a claimant state in international tribunals have historically been rejected by the losing party when core territorial claims are involved, meaning such rulings have tended to shape diplomatic and legal leverage over years rather than immediately resolve the dispute.

Long-running territorial disputes in contested waters have historically constrained joint oil and gas exploration in the same areas, since companies are typically reluctant to invest amid unresolved sovereignty claims.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Philippines v. China Permanent Court of Arbitration case (2013–2016): China rejected the ruling as null and void and continued its island-building and patrol activities in the disputed waters. The ruling did not resolve the underlying dispute, and multiple claimant states (Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei, Taiwan) continue to assert overlapping claims to parts of the same waters, through which a large share of global seaborne trade transits. Escalation of naval or coast guard confrontations in the South China Sea has historically raised shipping insurers' and carriers' attention to route risk in a corridor that carries a very large share of world seaborne trade, given the absence, so far, of a sustained blockade in the disputed waters.

linked_playbooks.name: Critical shipping route disruption
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Houthi attacks on commercial shipping in the Red Sea (Late 2023 – ongoing): Many major shipping lines rerouted around Africa's Cape of Good Hope, adding roughly 10–14 days to typical Asia–Europe voyages and pushing container freight rates sharply higher on affected routes. Disruption to a major shipping chokepoint has historically forced vessels onto longer alternate routes, raising fuel and time costs that carriers have often passed on as higher freight rates.

linked_playbooks.name: International court ruling on a territorial or trade dispute
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Philippines v. China South China Sea arbitration (2013–2016): China rejected the ruling outright and continued its activities in the disputed waters, showing that, unlike the Bakassi case where the losing party ultimately complied, an international ruling does not automatically compel compliance from a major power that rejects the tribunal's jurisdiction. International court rulings on territorial or maritime disputes have historically been complied with when the losing government has a political and diplomatic interest in maintaining its standing with the court system, as in the Bakassi case, but have been rejected outright by major powers unwilling to accept binding third-party jurisdiction over sovereignty claims, as in the South China Sea case.

linked_playbooks.name: Taiwan Strait military and political tension
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: China's military exercises following U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's visit to Taiwan (August 2022): Airlines and shipping operators rerouted some flights and vessels around the announced exercise and exclusion zones surrounding Taiwan for the duration of the drills. Periods of heightened Taiwan Strait tension have historically prompted temporary rerouting of commercial shipping and air traffic around announced exercise or exclusion zones, given Taiwan's location on major East Asia air and sea routes.

signals.headline: US suspending Microsoft from foreign worker visa programme

ripple_effect.name: Skilled-worker visa policy shift

historical_precedents.event: Trump administration's suspension of H-1B and other work-visa entry
historical_precedents.what_happened: Citing the risk that visa holders would "displace and disadvantage" US workers during the pandemic-era economic recovery, President Trump signed a proclamation on April 22, 2020 suspending entry for several nonimmigrant visa categories including H-1B, extended it through December 31, 2020, then again through March 31, 2021, before President Biden allowed the suspension to expire on April 1, 2021.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The roughly year-long suspension left many US employers, especially in technology, unable to bring new H-1B hires into the country during the suspension window, adding to pandemic-era hiring disruption for visa-dependent roles.

historical_precedents.event: $100,000 H-1B application fee
historical_precedents.what_happened: President Trump signed a proclamation requiring employers to pay a one-time $100,000 fee for new H-1B petitions filed between September 21, 2025 and September 21, 2026 — a roughly 65-fold increase over the prior ~$1,500 filing cost — with waivers available only where the Department of Homeland Security judged the hire to be in the national interest.
historical_precedents.market_impact: A federal judge ruled the $100,000 fee unlawful on June 8, 2026, but the year-plus of uncertainty in between affected employer hiring and budget planning for new skilled-visa hires, particularly in technology and healthcare roles that rely heavily on the H-1B category.

possibility_chains: A sudden increase in the cost or difficulty of hiring skilled foreign workers has historically pushed some employers to shift new hiring or entire teams to countries with more accessible immigration systems, a process that has typically played out over a year or more rather than immediately.

Restrictions on skilled-worker visas have historically had a concentrated impact on the specific industries (technology, healthcare, academia) that rely most heavily on that visa category, rather than spreading evenly across the labor market.

Because a large share of skilled-visa holders are early in their careers, sudden restrictions have historically had a disproportionate effect on entry-level hiring pipelines at affected employers, showing up gradually as those cohorts would otherwise have been promoted into more senior roles.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: $100,000 H-1B application fee (19 September 2025 – ongoing): A federal judge ruled the $100,000 fee unlawful on June 8, 2026, but the year-plus of uncertainty in between affected employer hiring and budget planning for new skilled-visa hires, particularly in technology and healthcare roles that rely heavily on the H-1B category. A sudden increase in the cost or difficulty of hiring skilled foreign workers has historically pushed some employers to shift new hiring or entire teams to countries with more accessible immigration systems, a process that has typically played out over a year or more rather than immediately.

linked_playbooks.name: Large-scale tech industry layoffs
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Elon Musk's mass layoffs at Twitter after his acquisition (November 2022 – April 2023): By January 2023 Twitter's headcount had fallen to roughly 2,300, and by April 2023 fewer than 1,500 active employees remained — an approximately 80% reduction from pre-acquisition levels — while the company also faced worker lawsuits alleging inadequate notice under the WARN Act. A wave of layoffs at one large tech employer has historically been followed within months by similar cuts at competitors, as boards and investors reward visible cost discipline during the same macro conditions.

linked_playbooks.name: Agricultural guest-worker / farm labor immigration policy shift
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Growth of the H-2A agricultural guest-worker visa program (1997–2020): By the late 2010s several major farm states (North Carolina, Washington, Florida, Georgia, California) had come to rely on H-2A workers for more than half of their certified agricultural labor positions, making the program a structural feature of US farm labor supply rather than a marginal one — and making farm output in those states sensitive to any future federal changes to the visa's rules or processing speed. Tightening immigration enforcement or guest-worker visa availability in a major agricultural region has historically raised the risk of unharvested crops and higher farm labor costs during peak harvest windows, since domestic labor has rarely fully filled the resulting gap on short notice.

ripple_effect.name: Minimum wage policy shift

historical_precedents.event: "Fight for $15" movement
historical_precedents.what_happened: The movement began in November 2012 when over 100 fast-food workers walked off the job in New York City demanding a $15 hourly wage and the right to unionize, at a time when the federal minimum wage had been frozen at $7.25 since 2009; it grew into coordinated multi-city strikes, including an April 2015 day of action across more than 200 cities that organizers called the largest protest by low-wage workers in US history.
historical_precedents.market_impact: By the mid-2020s seventeen US states plus Washington, D.C. had adopted $15-or-higher minimum wages, with organizers estimating roughly 26 million workers received a combined $151 billion in raises traceable to the movement's pressure on state and local policy.

historical_precedents.event: Seattle becomes the first major US city to adopt a $15 minimum wage
historical_precedents.what_happened: Seattle's city council, led by councilmember Kshama Sawant, passed an ordinance phasing in a $15 minimum wage starting in 2014, with the wage rising further to $15.45 in 2018 and $16 in 2019 under the city's indexing formula.
historical_precedents.market_impact: University of Washington and other researchers studying Seattle's rollout found no measurable decline in overall employment as the wage floor rose, making Seattle a frequently cited case study in the broader minimum-wage debate.

possibility_chains: A minimum wage increase in one large city or state has historically prompted advocacy campaigns citing it as precedent for similar increases elsewhere, spreading policy change faster than pure economic modeling alone would predict.

Employers in low-margin, labor-intensive sectors (fast food, retail, hospitality) have historically responded to minimum wage increases through some combination of price increases, reduced hours, and accelerated investment in self-service or automation technology, with the mix varying by study and locality.
Higher minimum wages have historically raised the wage floor workers use as a reference point in unrelated wage negotiations nearby, a "lighthouse effect" observed in several minimum-wage studies.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Seattle becomes the first major US city to adopt a $15 minimum wage (2014–2019): University of Washington and other researchers studying Seattle's rollout found no measurable decline in overall employment as the wage floor rose, making Seattle a frequently cited case study in the broader minimum-wage debate. A minimum wage increase in one large city or state has historically prompted advocacy campaigns citing it as precedent for similar increases elsewhere, spreading policy change faster than pure economic modeling alone would predict.

linked_playbooks.name: Gig-economy worker classification ruling
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: California's Proposition 22 and its multi-year court challenge (November 2020 – July 2024): The nearly four-year legal uncertainty over Proposition 22's validity was itself a business risk for Uber, Lyft, DoorDash, and Instacart, which had spent over $200 million campaigning for the measure; its eventual affirmation cemented independent-contractor status for California gig drivers and became a template gig companies pushed for in other US states. A court or ballot-measure ruling on gig-worker classification in one jurisdiction has historically become a reference point cited by both labor advocates and gig companies lobbying for similar outcomes elsewhere, spreading the policy debate beyond the original jurisdiction.

linked_playbooks.name: Broad-based voluntary quits wave / labor shortage
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: The "Great Resignation" in the United States (March 2021 – mid-2023): Employers responded with the fastest wage growth in two decades — 4.5% year-over-year in December 2021 — while hospitality, healthcare, and education faced acute staffing shortages that pushed many businesses to accelerate investment in automation and self-service technology; quits rates did not return to pre-pandemic 2019 norms until mid-2023. A sustained period of unusually high voluntary quits has historically coincided with faster wage growth, as employers compete harder to retain and attract staff in a tight labor market.

ripple_effect.name: Nuclear or long-range missile test triggering international sanctions

historical_precedents.event: North Korea's sixth nuclear test and ICBM tests
historical_precedents.what_happened: North Korea conducted its sixth and largest nuclear test on 3 September 2017, with seismic activity assessed at roughly 10 times more powerful than its previous test and an estimated yield of around 250 kilotons; the U.S. Geological Survey recorded a magnitude 6.3 event. Earlier that year, North Korea also test-fired intercontinental ballistic missiles on 4 July and 28 July 2017 that analysts assessed were capable of reaching the continental United States.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The UN Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 2375 on 11 September 2017, capping North Korea's refined petroleum imports (initially 500,000 barrels over three months, then 2 million barrels annually), banning all textile exports (an estimated $800 million annual revenue loss), and phasing out visas for North Korean overseas workers (estimated to cost North Korea another $500 million a year) — among the most restrictive sanctions the Council had imposed on the country to that point.

possibility_chains: A major nuclear or long-range missile test has historically prompted the UN Security Council to negotiate new sanctions resolutions in the following days to weeks, though the scope of sanctions has depended on securing agreement from all five permanent members, including the tested country's key trading partners.

Sanctions that target a specific export sector, such as textiles, or a labor-export revenue stream have historically been calibrated to cut off specific, identifiable sources of foreign currency earnings for the sanctioned government.

Repeated missile and nuclear tests over time have historically produced diminishing market and diplomatic reaction with each subsequent test, as neighboring countries and investors adjust to a higher baseline level of tension.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: North Korea's sixth nuclear test and ICBM tests (2017): The UN Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 2375 on 11 September 2017, capping North Korea's refined petroleum imports (initially 500,000 barrels over three months, then 2 million barrels annually), banning all textile exports (an estimated $800 million annual revenue loss), and phasing out visas for North Korean overseas workers (estimated to cost North Korea another $500 million a year) — among the most restrictive sanctions the Council had imposed on the country to that point. A major nuclear or long-range missile test has historically prompted the UN Security Council to negotiate new sanctions resolutions in the following days to weeks, though the scope of sanctions has depended on securing agreement from all five permanent members, including the tested country's key trading partners.

linked_playbooks.name: Major arms control treaty withdrawal or collapse

linked_playbooks.name: Sanctions imposed on a major economy

historical_precedents.event: Nord Stream pipeline sabotage

historical_precedents.market_impact: European natural gas benchmark prices, which had already surged to record highs earlier in 2022 as Russian pipeline supply fell, remained elevated; European governments accelerated efforts to secure LNG imports and other pipeline gas to replace the lost Russian route, and neither pipeline had been repaired as of the most recent public reporting.

historical_precedents.event: Russia-Ukraine gas transit dispute
historical_precedents.what_happened: A pricing and debt dispute between Gazprom and Ukraine's Naftogaz led Russia to halt all gas flows through Ukraine's pipeline network — then the main route for Russian gas to Europe — for about 13 days.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Bulgaria, Slovakia, and several Balkan and Southeastern European countries lost the large majority of their gas supply; Bulgaria had to halt production at some industrial plants and Slovakia declared a state of emergency, while Gazprom and Ukraine each lost an estimated hundreds of millions to over a billion dollars in revenue and transit fees.

Sustained higher natural gas costs have historically raised electricity prices in gas-reliant power grids and increased costs for gas-intensive industries such as fertilizer and chemicals production.

ripple_effect.name: Coup or abrupt regime change disrupting trade relationships

historical_precedents.event: Niger military coup
historical_precedents.what_happened: On 26 July 2023, General Abdourahamane Tchiani led the presidential guard in removing President Mohamed Bazoum and installed a military council. The regional bloc ECOWAS responded with an ultimatum, then sanctions including closed land and air borders, a no-fly zone on commercial flights, suspension of financial transactions, and asset freezes; Nigeria cut electricity supply to Niger on 2 August 2023.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The West African regional central bank cancelled a planned 30 billion CFA franc (about $51 million) bond issuance for Niger, and the World Bank suspended disbursements to the country. Niger is a significant global uranium exporter, and the coup raised questions over the operations of French nuclear fuel company Orano's mining activities there.

historical_precedents.event: Myanmar military coup
historical_precedents.what_happened: Senior General Min Aung Hlaing seized power on 1 February 2021, detaining civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi and other elected officials. The Biden administration imposed sanctions on military leaders on 11 February 2021 and froze $1 billion in Myanmar government assets held in the U.S.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Foreign direct investment into Myanmar fell 22% to $3.8 billion in fiscal year 2020, and major foreign investors withdrew: Japan's Kirin ended a $1.7 billion brewery joint venture, Thailand's Amata halted a $1 billion industrial zone project, and India's Adani Ports terminated a $127 million port investment. The Yangon Stock Exchange suspended trading, and property sales reportedly dropped by nearly 100%.

ripple_effect.name: Low-cost carriers disrupt legacy airline pricing after deregulation

historical_precedents.event: Ryanair adopts the low-cost carrier model as EU aviation deregulation takes effect
historical_precedents.what_happened: Ryanair restructured itself into a low-cost carrier starting in 1990, after its founders studied Southwest Airlines' model in the United States; the airline standardized on an all-Boeing 737 fleet and cut its cheapest return fare from £99 to £59. When Ryanair had launched its Dublin-London Luton route in 1987 under partial EEC air-travel deregulation, it priced return fares at £99 — roughly half the prevailing legacy-carrier rate — prompting Aer Lingus and British Airways to cut their own fares to £95 and £94.99 in response. The EU's Single Aviation Market, established in 1992, and further deregulation in April 1997 removed remaining cabotage restrictions and enabled Ryanair's rapid pan-European expansion, with annual passengers growing from about 745,000 in 1990 to 66.5 million by 2010.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Ryanair's model was subsequently adopted by other low-cost carriers including easyJet, WestJet, and AirAsia, restructuring competitive pricing across the European aviation market over the following decades.

historical_precedents.event: US Airline Deregulation Act and the growth of low-cost, point-to-point carriers
historical_precedents.what_happened: Following the 1978 US Airline Deregulation Act, low-cost carriers such as Southwest Airlines expanded point-to-point service that competed directly with legacy hub-and-spoke carriers on price.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Average US fares per passenger mile fell about 9% between 1979 and 1994, and inflation-adjusted fares fell roughly 30% between 1976 and 1990; a New York-Los Angeles round trip that would have cost an inflation-adjusted $1,442 in 1974 could be purchased for around $268 by 2010, though these savings accrued more to higher-traffic, longer-distance routes than to shorter ones.

possibility_chains: A low-cost carrier entering a new route or market has historically forced incumbent legacy carriers to cut their own fares on that route in direct response, rather than cede the market entirely.

Sustained low-cost-carrier competition following deregulation has historically compressed average industry fares over a period of years to decades, with the effect concentrated on the routes most exposed to new low-cost entrants.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: US Airline Deregulation Act and the growth of low-cost, point-to-point carriers (1978–1994): Average US fares per passenger mile fell about 9% between 1979 and 1994, and inflation-adjusted fares fell roughly 30% between 1976 and 1990; a New York-Los Angeles round trip that would have cost an inflation-adjusted $1,442 in 1974 could be purchased for around $268 by 2010, though these savings accrued more to higher-traffic, longer-distance routes than to shorter ones. A low-cost carrier entering a new route or market has historically forced incumbent legacy carriers to cut their own fares on that route in direct response, rather than cede the market entirely.

linked_playbooks.name: 2008–2015 US airline merger wave consolidates the industry into four major carriers
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: American Airlines merges with US Airways (February–December 2013): The merger created what became, by some measurements, the largest airline in the world by passengers carried and scheduled passenger-kilometers flown, completing a consolidation wave that also included United Airlines' 2010 merger with Continental — leaving the US domestic market dominated by four major carriers (American, Delta, United, and Southwest). A period of sustained high fuel costs or post-recession financial stress has historically accelerated airline merger activity, as weaker carriers sought scale and stronger balance sheets through consolidation rather than standalone survival.

linked_playbooks.name: Thomas Cook collapse triggers UK's largest peacetime repatriation
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Collapse of Thomas Cook Group (September 2019): The UK Civil Aviation Authority launched 'Operation Matterhorn,' chartering roughly 40 aircraft from other carriers including easyJet, Virgin Atlantic, and Malaysia Airlines to repatriate stranded travelers — an operation the CAA said overtook the 2017 collapse of Monarch Airlines as the UK's largest peacetime repatriation. About 21,000 Thomas Cook employees worldwide lost their jobs, including 9,000 in the UK; the company had reported a £1.5 billion loss for the first half of 2019, including £1.1 billion in goodwill write-downs. A major tour operator or airline's sudden collapse has historically stranded large numbers of travelers simultaneously, forcing government-coordinated emergency repatriation using capacity chartered from competing airlines.

historical_precedents.event: Iran–Iraq "Tanker War"

historical_precedents.market_impact: Oil prices roughly doubled in the months following the invasion before falling back once the war ended and supply concerns eased.

possibility_chains: Roughly a fifth of the world's oil is estimated to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, so a sustained blockage or major disruption there has historically driven crude oil prices sharply higher.

ripple_effect.name: Remittance-dependent economies and diaspora labor migration

historical_precedents.event: Tajikistan's remittance dependence peaks among the world's highest
historical_precedents.what_happened: Remittances, sent primarily by Tajik labor migrants working in Russia, made up about 48% of Tajikistan's GDP in 2024, one of the highest remittance-to-GDP ratios of any country.
historical_precedents.market_impact: This level of dependence has historically made Tajikistan's economy highly sensitive to labor-market and currency conditions in Russia: a slowdown in Russian labor demand, tighter migration policy, or a weaker ruble has fed directly through into reduced household income and foreign-currency inflows at home.

historical_precedents.event: Remittances exceed a quarter of GDP in multiple Asian and Latin American economies
historical_precedents.what_happened: World Bank-era estimates for 2023 put remittances at roughly 35% of GDP in Nepal, about 19.3% in Guatemala, and about 17.8% in Uzbekistan, while the Philippines — one of the largest recipients in absolute dollar terms — received remittances equal to roughly 9.2% of GDP that year.
historical_precedents.market_impact: In each of these economies, remittances functioned as a larger and comparatively more stable source of foreign currency than either foreign direct investment or official development aid, cushioning consumption during domestic downturns but also transmitting external labor-market shocks from destination countries.

historical_precedents.event: Global remittance flows grow more than tenfold over two decades
historical_precedents.what_happened: Global remittance flows rose from about $72.3 billion in 2001 to about $549 billion in 2019 and about $780 billion sent to roughly 800 million people in 2021.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The sustained growth in remittance flows made diaspora labor migration one of the largest channels of cross-border financial support to developing economies, growing faster over this period than global foreign direct investment flows to the same country group.

possibility_chains: A sharp slowdown in a major migrant-labor destination economy has historically reduced remittance inflows to dependent source countries with a lag of a few months, since migrants have tended to draw down savings or reduce discretionary transfers before returning home outright.

Because remittances are typically spent on household consumption rather than invested in productive capacity, remittance-dependent economies have historically shown resilient consumer spending during global downturns but have also shown limited translation of remittance inflows into broad-based domestic investment or export diversification.

A currency devaluation in a remittance-dependent recipient country has historically increased the local-currency value of a fixed dollar remittance, temporarily boosting recipient households' purchasing power even as the devaluation raises the cost of imported goods economy-wide.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Global remittance flows grow more than tenfold over two decades (2001–2021): The sustained growth in remittance flows made diaspora labor migration one of the largest channels of cross-border financial support to developing economies, growing faster over this period than global foreign direct investment flows to the same country group. A sharp slowdown in a major migrant-labor destination economy has historically reduced remittance inflows to dependent source countries with a lag of a few months, since migrants have tended to draw down savings or reduce discretionary transfers before returning home outright.

signals.headline: «Trump verachtet uns», sagt der Kanadier, der am «Lake America» lebt. «Er hält uns für Abtrünnige und Schmarotzer»

ripple_effect.name: Major tariff escalation / trade war

historical_precedents.event: U.S.–China trade war
historical_precedents.what_happened: The U.S. imposed tariffs on hundreds of billions of dollars of Chinese goods, and China retaliated with its own tariffs, including on U.S. agricultural exports.
historical_precedents.market_impact: U.S. soybean exports to China fell sharply, and the U.S. government paid out tens of billions of dollars in subsidies to farmers hurt by the retaliation; global manufacturers reported higher input costs and supply-chain uncertainty through the period.

historical_precedents.event: Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act
historical_precedents.what_happened: The U.S. raised tariffs on over 20,000 imported goods to some of the highest levels in a century; Canada, France, and other major trading partners retaliated with their own tariffs within months.
historical_precedents.market_impact: World trade volumes fell by roughly two-thirds over the following four years; widely cited by economists as having deepened and prolonged the Great Depression globally, not just in the U.S. — the clearest historical example that a major tariff escalation's damage isn't confined to the two countries directly involved.

historical_precedents.event: China's rare earth export restrictions on Japan
historical_precedents.what_happened: After Japan detained a Chinese trawler captain following a collision near the disputed Senkaku/Diaoyu Islands, China informally slowed rare earth mineral shipments to Japan without declaring a formal ban.
historical_precedents.market_impact: China's rare earth exports fell roughly 77% year-on-year by September 2011, and global prices spiked several-fold (cerium oxide rose from around $4.70/kg in April 2010 to around $36/kg that October). The U.S. filed a WTO case in 2012; the WTO ruled against China in 2014, and China dropped its export quotas in 2015 — but the episode had already pushed Japan and other importers to diversify sourcing and boost recycling.

possibility_chains: New tariffs have historically raised the cost of the affected imported goods, at least part of which has often been passed on to consumers or absorbed as lower profit margins by importers.
Retaliatory tariffs targeting a country's agricultural or manufacturing exports have historically hurt the specific industries and regions most exposed to that export market.

Extended periods of tariff uncertainty have historically led some companies to shift or diversify supply chains toward other countries, a process that has typically played out over one to several years, not weeks.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: China's rare earth export restrictions on Japan (September 2010 – 2011): China's rare earth exports fell roughly 77% year-on-year by September 2011, and global prices spiked several-fold (cerium oxide rose from around $4.70/kg in April 2010 to around $36/kg that October). The U.S. filed a WTO case in 2012; the WTO ruled against China in 2014, and China dropped its export quotas in 2015 — but the episode had already pushed Japan and other importers to diversify sourcing and boost recycling. New tariffs have historically raised the cost of the affected imported goods, at least part of which has often been passed on to consumers or absorbed as lower profit margins by importers.

ripple_effect.name: US territory / sub-sovereign debt restructuring crisis

historical_precedents.event: Puerto Rico's government-debt crisis and PROMESA restructuring
historical_precedents.what_happened: Puerto Rico's bonds were downgraded to junk status in February 2014, and Governor García Padilla declared the roughly $74 billion in bond debt (plus $49 billion in unfunded pension liabilities) 'not payable' on June 28, 2015; after Puerto Rico missed a $422 million payment on May 1, 2016, Congress passed PROMESA, which President Obama signed June 30, 2016, creating a federal oversight board with authority over the territory's budget and debt restructuring.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Puerto Rico's poverty rate reached roughly 45% by mid-2017, unemployment hit 12.4% in December 2016, and its sales tax rose to 11% alongside teacher retirement-age increases (47 to 62) and 10% pension cuts under the oversight board's austerity plan; nearly 70% of US municipal bond funds held Puerto Rico exposure, and its general obligation bonds fell to roughly 32 cents on the dollar after Hurricane Maria in 2017 before the territory exited bankruptcy in March 2022.

possibility_chains: A US territory's debt crisis has historically been resolved through federal oversight mechanisms different from either a state (which cannot file Chapter 9 the way cities can) or an independent country (which cannot access IMF facilities), creating restructuring rules unique to the territory's ambiguous status.

Heavy institutional exposure to a single distressed municipal issuer (in this case, via tax-exempt bond funds that concentrated Puerto Rico debt for its tax advantages) has historically transmitted a regional fiscal crisis into national investment portfolios far from the issuer itself.

Debt-crisis austerity measures layered on top of a shrinking population and tax base have historically been self-reinforcing, since tax increases and service cuts have tended to accelerate the outward migration that shrank the tax base in the first place.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Puerto Rico's government-debt crisis and PROMESA restructuring (2014–2022): Puerto Rico's poverty rate reached roughly 45% by mid-2017, unemployment hit 12.4% in December 2016, and its sales tax rose to 11% alongside teacher retirement-age increases (47 to 62) and 10% pension cuts under the oversight board's austerity plan; nearly 70% of US municipal bond funds held Puerto Rico exposure, and its general obligation bonds fell to roughly 32 cents on the dollar after Hurricane Maria in 2017 before the territory exited bankruptcy in March 2022. A US territory's debt crisis has historically been resolved through federal oversight mechanisms different from either a state (which cannot file Chapter 9 the way cities can) or an independent country (which cannot access IMF facilities), creating restructuring rules unique to the territory's ambiguous status.

linked_playbooks.name: Major municipal or county bankruptcy
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Jefferson County, Alabama bankruptcy (November 2011 – December 2013): The county cut its government workforce by more than 700 employees by May 2012, and the bankruptcy court wrote off more than $1.4 billion of the debt before the county emerged from bankruptcy in December 2013. A municipal bankruptcy driven by a shrinking tax base and rising legacy retiree costs has historically forced a choice between deep pension cuts and finding outside funding (such as philanthropic support) to soften them, since the two options are not fiscally separable.

linked_playbooks.name: Government austerity program (spending cuts and tax rises)
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Canada's 1995 federal budget under Finance Minister Paul Martin (1995): By shrinking the federal transfer, the reform shifted fiscal pressure onto provincial governments, which had to make their own cuts to health and social assistance spending to absorb the reduced federal contribution. Government austerity programs that cut public sector employment have historically taken years to fully play out in local labor markets, as affected workers and the local businesses that served them adjust gradually rather than all at once.

linked_playbooks.name: Sovereign government debt default
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Sri Lanka's first sovereign default (April 2022): The default followed foreign reserves falling to just $1.9 billion by March 2022, insufficient to cover the country's import and debt-service needs, and led into an IMF rescue program. A sovereign default has historically triggered a sharp loss of access to international capital markets for the defaulting government, often for years, forcing reliance on domestic financing or multilateral lenders in the interim.

signals.headline: Planned Pension Age Increase Again Raises Public Concern

ripple_effect.name: Retirement age / pension reform and backlash

historical_precedents.event: France's 2023 pension reform and nationwide strikes
historical_precedents.what_happened: The French government proposed raising the legal retirement age from 62 to 64 and increasing the required contribution period from 42 to 43 years; over one million people demonstrated nationwide on January 19, 2023, with subsequent protest days drawing anywhere from several hundred thousand to (by union counts) 2–2.5 million people. On March 16, 2023, Prime Minister Élisabeth Borne invoked Article 49.3 of the constitution to force the bill through without a parliamentary vote, triggering further protests and two no-confidence motions that narrowly failed.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The reform was ultimately enacted despite the sustained opposition, but the government's use of Article 49.3 rather than a parliamentary majority became a lasting point of political controversy, and the episode weighed on President Macron's approval ratings and his coalition's ability to pass subsequent legislation in a parliament where it had already lost its outright majority.

possibility_chains: Government proposals to raise the retirement age have historically triggered some of the largest and most sustained street protests of a given political cycle, since the policy directly and visibly affects a large share of the working population's near-term life plans.

Where a government lacks a legislative majority, forcing a retirement-age or pension reform through by decree or special procedure has historically deepened, rather than resolved, the underlying political conflict, leaving lasting effects on the government's ability to pass unrelated legislation.

Pension and retirement-age reforms have historically interacted with demographic pressure (a shrinking ratio of working-age contributors to retirees) as the underlying economic justification, even when the political debate has focused primarily on fairness and timing.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: France's 2023 pension reform and nationwide strikes (January–June 2023): The reform was ultimately enacted despite the sustained opposition, but the government's use of Article 49.3 rather than a parliamentary majority became a lasting point of political controversy, and the episode weighed on President Macron's approval ratings and his coalition's ability to pass subsequent legislation in a parliament where it had already lost its outright majority. Government proposals to raise the retirement age have historically triggered some of the largest and most sustained street protests of a given political cycle, since the policy directly and visibly affects a large share of the working population's near-term life plans.

linked_playbooks.name: Inflation-driven public-sector/transport strike wave
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: 2022–2024 UK railway strikes (21 June 2022 – November 2024): Strike days cut services to roughly 20% of normal timetabled capacity, and the hospitality sector estimated £1.5 billion in lost trade over the dispute; the UK's Conservative government blocked settlement in England for an extended period even as devolved Scottish and Welsh disputes were resolved by May 2023, with final agreement in England only reached after the 2024 change of government, when workers secured improved pay and the cancellation of proposed ticket-office closures. A period of high inflation eroding real wages has historically produced a wave of strikes across multiple public-facing sectors in the same country within the same one-to-two-year window, rather than an isolated dispute in a single industry.

ripple_effect.name: Persian Gulf oil supply shock

historical_precedents.event: Iran–Iraq "Tanker War"
historical_precedents.what_happened: Iran and Iraq attacked oil tankers transiting the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz, and Iran repeatedly threatened to close the strait.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Shipping insurance war-risk premiums in the Gulf rose sharply, and the U.S. Navy began escorting reflagged Kuwaiti tankers in 1987 to keep the strait open.

historical_precedents.event: Drone and missile attack on Saudi Aramco's Abqaiq and Khurais facilities
historical_precedents.what_happened: The attack (which Saudi Arabia and the U.S. blamed on Iran, a claim Iran denied) temporarily knocked out roughly half of Saudi Arabia's oil output, about 5% of global supply.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Brent crude jumped about 15% in a single day — the largest one-day oil price increase since the 1990–91 Gulf War.

historical_precedents.event: Gulf War (Iraqi invasion of Kuwait)
historical_precedents.what_happened: Iraq's invasion of Kuwait removed a large share of Gulf oil exports from the market and raised fears of a wider regional war.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Oil prices roughly doubled in the months following the invasion before falling back once the war ended and supply concerns eased.

possibility_chains: Roughly a fifth of the world's oil is estimated to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, so a sustained blockage or major disruption there has historically driven crude oil prices sharply higher.

Because ammonia-based fertilizer production is natural-gas intensive, and natural gas prices often move together with oil, a prolonged energy price spike has historically fed through into higher fertilizer costs over the following months.
Fertilizer is a major input cost in food production, so energy shocks of this kind have historically been followed — often with a lag — by higher food prices.
Shipping insurers have historically raised war-risk premiums for vessels transiting the Gulf during periods of heightened tension, adding to the landed cost of oil and other cargo.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Gulf War (Iraqi invasion of Kuwait) (1990–1991): Oil prices roughly doubled in the months following the invasion before falling back once the war ended and supply concerns eased. Roughly a fifth of the world's oil is estimated to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, so a sustained blockage or major disruption there has historically driven crude oil prices sharply higher.
